subject: microbiology
title: Varicella Zoster Virus, Shingles and Cytomegalovirus

steps.tx: **Varicella zoster virus** causes chickenpox during primary infection and herpes zoster after latency in dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia. Varicella is highly contagious by airborne spread and lesion contact. Zoster follows declining cell mediated immunity with age or immunosuppression. The same virus therefore creates a diffuse childhood exanthem and a localised dermatomal eruption decades later.
steps.say: Chickenpox is first infection; shingles is VZV waking in one ganglion.

left.title: Varicella
points: Generalised itchy lesions in different stages
Macules, vesicles and crusts coexist
More severe in adults and pregnancy
Airborne precautions for susceptible inpatients

right.title: Zoster
points: Pain may precede rash by days
Unilateral dermatomal vesicles
Does not normally cross midline
Postherpetic neuralgia can persist for months

steps.tx: **Shingles** diagnosis is usually clinical, but PCR helps in atypical, disseminated or zoster sine herpete presentations where pain occurs without rash. Vesicles should be unroofed and the base swabbed. Antivirals work best within seventy two hours yet remain indicated later if new lesions, eye involvement or immunocompromise are present. Pain control is a treatment goal from the first day, not an afterthought.
steps.say: A dermatomal vesicular rash needs early antiviral therapy and deliberate pain control.

left.title: Urgent features
points: Hutchinson sign suggests nasociliary eye risk
Ramsay Hunt syndrome affects ear and facial nerve
Dissemination beyond primary and adjacent dermatomes
Visceral disease in profound immunosuppression

right.title: Management
points: Valacyclovir or acyclovir promptly
Ophthalmology for eye involvement
Analgesia including neuropathic agents when needed
Recombinant zoster vaccine for prevention in eligible adults

steps.tx: **Cytomegalovirus** is a beta herpesvirus that establishes latency in myeloid progenitors and persists in many tissues. Most immunocompetent infections are silent or cause a mononucleosis-like illness with negative heterophile tests. Reactivation or primary infection in transplant recipients and advanced HIV can cause retinitis, colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis and graft injury. Tissue invasive disease requires compatible organ signs plus histology or validated molecular evidence.
steps.say: CMV is quiet in healthy hosts and an organ-by-organ opportunist when T cell control fails.

left.title: Hosts at risk
points: Solid organ and stem cell transplant recipients
Advanced HIV
Fetus after maternal primary infection
Critically ill immunocompetent patients occasionally

right.title: Organ disease
points: Retinitis threatening sight
Colitis with ulceration and bleeding
Pneumonitis especially after stem cell transplant
Hepatitis, encephalitis and marrow suppression

steps.tx: CMV infected cells enlarge with a basophilic intranuclear **owl eye inclusion** and smaller cytoplasmic inclusions. Histology remains valuable in colitis and pneumonitis because blood viral load alone cannot prove which organ is invaded. Quantitative CMV DNA monitoring guides pre emptive therapy after transplantation; thresholds and kinetics differ by assay and organ risk, so trends must be interpreted with a single validated platform where possible.
steps.say: Owl eye cells prove CMV in tissue; blood viral load shows systemic replication pressure.

left.title: Tissue proof
points: Cytomegalic cells with nuclear inclusion
Halo around inclusion creates owl eye
Immunohistochemistry increases sensitivity
Biopsy site must match clinical syndrome

right.title: Blood monitoring
points: Quantitative PCR in plasma or whole blood
Rising trend can trigger preemptive therapy
Prophylaxis used in highest risk transplants
Low level DNAemia is not automatically organ disease

steps.tx: **Congenital CMV** is the leading infectious cause of sensorineural hearing loss and neurodevelopmental injury in many settings. Maternal primary infection carries higher transmission risk than reactivation, but preexisting immunity does not eliminate fetal disease. Newborn saliva or urine PCR within the first three weeks distinguishes congenital from postnatal acquisition. Hearing follow up remains necessary even when the newborn examination is normal.
steps.say: A positive CMV test after three weeks cannot prove congenital infection; test early and follow hearing.

nodes.label: Urine or saliva PCR by three weeks
Serial hearing and developmental follow up

steps.tx: Ganciclovir and valganciclovir inhibit CMV DNA synthesis after initial phosphorylation, but can cause neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Foscarnet and cidofovir are alternatives with nephrotoxicity. **Letermovir** inhibits the terminase complex and is used for prophylaxis in defined transplant groups, not as a universal treatment. **Maribavir** targets the viral kinase and has a role in refractory or resistant CMV under specialist direction.
steps.say: CMV drugs trade antiviral power against marrow and kidney toxicity, so monitoring is inseparable.

left.title: Treatment backbone
points: IV ganciclovir for severe disease
Oral valganciclovir for many stable patients
Monitor full blood count and renal function
Reduce immunosuppression where feasible

right.title: Special situations
points: Foscarnet for UL97 resistance or marrow intolerance
Cidofovir needs renal protection strategies
Letermovir mainly prophylaxis in eligible transplant recipients
Resistance genotyping guides refractory disease
